qt: to the Commission Konstantinos Arvanitis (The Left) Subject:

Today, a BBC article1 revealed that Greek law enforcement authorities have been using migrants to assist them in large-scale pushback operations targeting hundreds of other migrants each week at the country’s land border with Türkiye. Masked mercenaries are recruited from countries such as Pakistan, Syria and Afghanistan, and rewarded with cash, valuables and mobile phones looted from other migrants, as well as with papers allowing them passage through Greece. Confirming earlier (2022) allegations by Lighthouse Reports and Frontex’s Fundamental Rights Office itself, the article refers to internal police documents describing the informal recruitment of so-called migrant mercenaries as early as 2020, as ordered and overseen by senior officers. The BBC’s findings include allegations of extreme violence, with testimonies indicating that migrants and asylum seekers have been stripped, robbed, beaten until they passed out, and even sexually assaulted. Although the Greek Prime Minister claimed that he was unaware of the allegations about the use of mercenaries, the investigative team’s police sources asserted that ‘there is no soldier, police officer or Frontex officer serving here in Evros who does not know that pushbacks are taking place.’ Can the Commission therefore answer the following questions: 1.
What action does it intend to take in response to these allegations?
What measures could it take to improve early intervention and deterrence procedures in similar/related cases?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.10.2026) The Commission takes allegations of fundamental rights violations at the EU’s external borders very seriously. Investigating individual allegations of violence, exploitation or other abuses, and establishing any criminal responsibility, falls primarily within the competence of the relevant national authorities, including the judicial authorities. All activities carried out by Member States in the context of border management must comply with EU and international law, including the principle of non-refoulement and respect for fundamental rights. It is primarily for Member States to take the necessary measures to prevent, detect and address possible fundamental rights violations in the context of border management. The Pact on Migration and Asylum1, which entered into application on 12 June 2026, requires Member States to establish an independent monitoring mechanism covering screening2 and the asylum border procedure3 and to put in place the national arrangements necessary to ensure compliance with EU law. The Commission will monitor the implementation of these requirements and may, where appropriate, take action in accordance with its role as guardian of the Treaties.
1 https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies/migration-and-asylum/pact-migration-and-asylum_en. 2 Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1356 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024

introducing the screening of third-country nationals at the external borders and amending Regulations (EC) No 767/2008, (EU) 2017/2226, (EU) 2018/1240 and (EU) 2019/817; ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1356/oj. 3 Article 43 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1348 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 establishing a common procedure for international protection in the Union and repealing Directive 2013/32/EU; ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1348/oj.
